title: From reading to writing - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

DNA writing is entering a period of rapid innovation, with enzymatic and cellular approaches challenging decades-old chemistry. Although none yet delivers long, accurate DNA at the scale biology ultimately requires, continued advances promise to remove one of the field’s most persistent bottlenecks and enable experiments that are currently out of reach.

For the past two decades, our ability to read and edit DNA has transformed biology, fueled by advances in sequencing technology, gene editing tools and computational methods. Yet writing DNA from scratch is still a bottleneck for biotechnology, especially the synthesis of long, complex sequences and libraries. Currently, there are four major classes of DNA synthesis technologies, solving different parts of the DNA writing process; however, each comes with limitations.Phosphoramidite chemistry, the industry standard, can generate DNA oligo sequences up to 200 nucleotides in length, and the workflow is essentially unchanged since the early 1980s1. The method involves a four-step cycle to deblock the terminal nucleotide, activate and couple with an additional nucleotide, cap the end to avoid another addition, and oxidize for stability. While each step is highly efficient, applying hundreds of cycles eventually causes error rates to become limiting.There are new ways to assemble these shorter oligos into longer, more complex DNA sequences or plasmids. Earlier this year, a group introduced a three-way junction technique called Sidewinder2. Instead of relying on overlapping ends for DNA assembly of fragments, Sidewinder contains a third strand that carries information about the order of fragment assembly, and this strand never becomes part of the finished product. The method works well on sequences that are difficult to assemble with overlap-based methods, like repetitive sequences. This month in Nature Biotechnology, Wu et. al. present Molecular Self-Assembly Induced Cloning (MOSAIC), a different approach to generating long DNA sequences that couples programmable self-assembly of oligos with cellular DNA nick repair machinery3. In MOSAIC, overlapping oligos self-assemble in a one-pot reaction in vitro, and DNA nick repair machinery in vivo seals nicks to create functional plasmid constructs, even with difficult-to-assemble sequences. These methods both advance DNA assembly (length and speed), but cannot correct synthesis errors in the original oligo sequences used, which are still generated chemically.For production of synthetic DNA without the use of oligos, there are enzymatic approaches. Instead of using chemical cycles to add nucleotides, enzymes such as terminal deoxynucleotidal transferase (TdT) add nucleotides one at a time, without needing any template. Ansa Biotechnologies has shown that it can use TdT conjugated to a single nucleotide to directly synthesize DNA molecules over 1,000 bases long without assembling shorter oligos4. Each synthesis cycle adds one specified nucleotide, and then the enzyme is removed and the process repeats. The enzymatic technology is sequence agnostic — the chemistry does not inherently depend on the identity of the next base or on local sequence context, unlike some other DNA synthesis methods — but still has a small error rate of about 1 error per 1,000 bases. Other companies are looking for other enzymatic options. Camena Bioscience instead uses an optimized mix of enzymes to build DNA fragments and then assemble them. Their specific enzymes, however, are proprietary, and their data have not yet been published.Large DNA sequences can theoretically also be completely assembled or replicated in vivo by retrons — bacterial genetic elements that can produce single-stranded DNA inside cells using an RNA template. In this method, a retron containing a reverse transcriptase and an RNA template are encoded in a plasmid and delivered to a cell, which then uses its own machinery to generate corresponding single-stranded DNA. While the idea has potential, retrons have only been used so far to generate short sequences of tens of base pairs. To turn this into programmable, intracellular DNA writing, the system would need a polymerase or reverse transcriptase capable of producing much longer DNA, robust error correction, and a way to assemble and then recover these products efficiently.Efficient and reliable DNA writing technologies would have major opportunities in the therapeutic space. The best commercial opportunity is probably therapeutic DNA manufacturing — complete replacement of phosphoramidite synthesis for DNA used in CRISPR therapeutics, gene therapy, CAR-T engineering and more. Artificial intelligence is driving protein engineering, but to express a designed protein, a DNA sequence needs to exist. With faster and cheaper DNA writing, the experimental loop for AI protein design accelerates. Cell therapies are becoming more complicated, involving multiple edits, synthetic promoters, safety switches and large knock-ins. Long, accurate DNA writing expands this design space. Finally, other, smaller areas of research such as assembling synthetic genomes from scratch, more ambitious pathway engineering for industry, DNA data storage, and molecular recording could all benefit from more advanced DNA writing technologies.As AI continues to accelerate the pace of experimental science, the need for DNA sequences will grow. Many laboratories can computationally design thousands of promising DNA constructs in hours, but physically building and testing them is the slowest and most expensive step. Reliability will be the key: when a sequence or plasmid is ordered from a commercial vendor, it needs to be correct. While companies report high accuracy rates for longer sequences, they still take too long to generate DNA products (weeks). The field needs to develop ways to make synthesis faster while also retaining accuracy.“As AI continues to accelerate the pace of experimental science, the need for DNA sequences will grow.”In addition, it is unlikely that these methods will be the end of the road. As new or modified enzymes or conceptually novel methods emerge, it will be necessary to have a DNA sequencing benchmark for reliability. To have commercial success, a new method will need to prove its technology against others on sequences of varied complexity and length. Success is not just about replacing phosphoramidite chemistry; it could enable faster progress in therapeutic development, protein engineering, synthetic biology and more advanced in vivo genome-writing systems. The next story is not how we will synthesize DNA, but what becomes possible once writing biology is as routine as reading it.
